SPECIAL MENTIONS  
Demand to declare underground fire in Jharia Coal Field a National Disaster  
SHRIMATI BRINDA KARAT (West Bengal): Sir, I draw th e special attention of the 
House towards the situation prevailing in 600 squar e kilometres of Jharia Coal Field area 
affecting 7 lakh people in Jharkhand and Raniganj C oalfield area in West Bengal due to 
underground fire having serious social, economic, i nfrastructural and environmental 
consequences.  
Recently, I visited several places of Jharia fire affected area and seen men, women and 
children living in area where poisonous gas is emit ting, subsidence is taking place and 
underground fire coming out. Several railway tracks are under threat. Railway line and station 
through Jharia have already been closed. The RSP College in Jharia with its 6000 students 
and Jharia's Central Water Supply in 'Zone-1', according to the report of the Central Mining 
Research Institute, is under serious threat stating 'the rate of progress of fire in zone-1 is in 
the range of 8-3 metre per month'.  
Presently, the matter is being handled by the Coal Ministry through Coal PSUs, ECL and 
BCCL as operating agencies. The lackadaisical approach of Coal Ministry can be seen in the 
notice issued by BCCL to Jharia College to shift from its present location as they 'deem fit'. 
Thus, lakhs of affected people have become victims on both counts.  
I urge the Central Government to consider such a di saster as a national disaster and act 
accordingly before a huge tragedy occurs. I request the Prime Minister to personally intervene 
to ensure formation of -coordinating bodies of all concerned Union Ministries and Stated 
Governments aiming at protecting lives and liveliho od of all sections of affected people, 
environment and areas by controlling underground fi re as far as possible and wherever 
required, resettlement and rehabilitation of all sections of affected people. Thank you.

Demand to Review the Policy of Ban or Recruitment i n Government Offices  
SHRI MOINUL HASSAN (West Bengal): Sir, the Government's decision to extend the 
blanket ban on recruitment, introduced in 2001 for another three years is extremely deplorable 
and smacks of Government's unconcern about the unem ployment problem in the country. 
The reduction in the number of posts due to the arb itrary decision has been of the order of 
8 lakh during the period between 1.1.2001 to 1.1.2006. The downsizing, not only shut down 
the job opportunities for the young and educated youth in the country, it has also phenomenally 
increased the workload of the existing employees. D ue to abolition of posts and other 
downsizing exercises carried out by the Government,  the work assigned was increased 
manifold. To combat the situation, the administrati on has been resorting to recruitment of 
daily rated/casual workers. They presently constitu te about 25 per cent of the workforce. 
They are not even given subsistence wages and are b eing exploited with utter violation of 
labour laws in the country. There is no move to regularise all these employees. If this is the 
attitude of the Government which is supposed to protect the law of the land, then the future 
of this country is very bleak. Hence, I urge upon t he Government to withdraw the ban on 
recruitment and regularise the casual workers immediately.  

208   Special  [RAJYASABHA]  Mentions  
Problems being faced by Exporters at Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust  
SHRI RAHUL BAJAJ (Maharashtra): Sir, since the last two months Indian exporters 
have been facing problems at JNPT in prompt shipment of their goods. This is due to lack of 
space for storage of containers at the port. This leads to their inability to keep their 
commitment. This issue should be resolved quickly. It is also ironic that in this situation 
newer ports like Mundra are being under-utilised due to poor connectivity and shipping 
services.  
Need to streamline Public Distribution System in Jharkhand  
MS. MABLE REBELLO (Jharkhand): The Public Distribution System in the country, 
particularly, in tribal areas where illiterate and not yet empowered live, doesn't serve the 
purpose at all. The kerosene oil meant for the people is siphoned off to the tune of 75 per 
cent. Similarly, subsidised rice and wheat is also pilfered and targeted poor hardly get 25 per 
cent of their entitlement of the ration.  
The wholesale dealers appointed almost 30-50 years ago have a field day. In one tribal 
district of Gumla in Jharkhand, there are only three wholesale dealers of kerosene. They 
were appointed in 1955,1969 and 1975, when it was part of united Bihar.  
They never supply monthly quota of four litres of kerosene to the PDS cardholders. The 
poor are miserable and suffering tremendously because they are not able even to light their 
houses.  
The wholesale dealers and local distributors sell the kerosene in black market at an 
exorbitant price of Rs.30-40/- per litre, whereas the PDS holders are entitled to buy kerosene 
at Rs.10/- per litre. This black marketing of kerosene is a very well established business in 
India and it amounts to almost Rs.4,000-5,000 crore per annum. This kerosene is used to 
adulterate petrol and diesel. This needs to be stopped at any cost.  
This comes to request the Government of India to direct the State Government of Jharkhand 
to streamline the Public Distribution System and help the poor to get their entitlement of 
kerosene and other ration like wheat and rice at subsidised price through PDS.  
Request for approval of long-pending Rural Development Projects in Karnataka  
SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD (Karnataka): Sir, it is heartening to note that the Centre has 
enhanced its budgetary allocation for 2008-09 for rural development signifying its 
commitment to tackle the urban-rural divide.  
Most of the 21 long-pending project proposals submitted by the Government of Karnataka 
relate to Swarna Jayanti Gram Swaraj Yojna. The propsoed projects, involving an outaly of 
Rs. 200 crores, will cover dairy development, rural livelihood and employment generation, 
creating better rural marketing infrastructure and rehabilitation of Devadasis under the SGSY 
Schemes. The major component of this integrated project package relate to dairy development 
activities in Bangalore rural and urban areas and the districs of Mandya, Bellary, Uttar 
Kannada, Mysore, Hassan and Chamrajnagar calling for Centre's allocation of Rs. 60 crores 
with the contribution of district milk unions totalling Rs. 20 crores.  
I urge the Ministry of Rural Development, Government of India, to expedite sanction for 
the above projects to be taken up under the current Budget allocation for 2008-09.  

Mentions  [5 MARCH 2008]  209   Special 
 
Need to provide Dual Citizenship to N.R.Is  
SHRI TARLOCHAN SINGH (Haryana): Sir, we are happy that the Government of India 
has introduced a scheme of providing dual citizenship to the NRIs settled abroad. A separate 
Ministry of Overseas Indians has now started providing maximum facilities to them. But the 
Government, especially the Ministry of Home Affairs , has not yet come out with a proper 
policy how to satisfy every section of the people of Indian origin. In a reply to my question, 
the Government admitted that a large number of NRIs were sent back even with valid visas 
from our airports, last year. We never consider how much mental torture they suffer, along 
with financial loss, in such uncalled for actions. Every NRI is keen to attend the marriage 
and death of their close relatives. They are also k een to pay obience at religious places. 
Every Sikh is keen to come to Golden Temple, Amrits ar. But to get visa is a problem. I 
suggest that the Government should introduce a special policy for granting temporary visas 
for seven to ten days even to those who are not con sidered suitable to get normal visa. I 
further suggest that a meeting of Members of Parliament, region-wise, be called to discuss 
this urgent problem. The so-called black list of NRIs is creating a lot of resentment, and is 
also against the human rights.

Demand to Protect Olive Ridley Turtles in Orissa  
SHRIMATIKANIMOZHI (Tamil Nadu): Sir, Olive Ridley is a rate and threatened species 
of turtles found in the East Coast. The beaches of Orissa provide one of the last nesting 
grounds for the Olive Ridley turtles in the world. Trawling and offshore drilling for oil and 
gas has been blamed for the death of more than 1,00 ,000 Olive Ridley turtles, which have 
been washed ashore in the last ten years.  
To preserve endangered species is to save the entir e eco-system. It would be a grave 
injustice committed to the future generation if we do not conserve nature and its inhabitants 
who have an equal right to exist along with humans. 
Research has proved that irresponsible development has contributed to decline in the 
number of the Olive Ridley turtles. The building of  coastal structures, including walls or 
even fences, has become obstacles for these turtles which come to lay eggs on the beaches. 
Even lights and planting of exotic trees along the coasts confuse these turtles, specially, the 
hatchlings.  
I request the Government to intervene and protect t his fragile species from artificially 
created hazards and also protect the environment.

Request for recruitment of local people to Group 'D' posts in Railways  
SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY (Karnataka): Sir, this is regarding recruitment to 4,700 
Group 'D" posts in the Railways in Karnataka.  
The posts were not advertised in the local regional  Kannada language newspapers in 
Karnataka, but were advertised only in Hindi newspapers in Bihar and other States.  
The question papers were allegedly set in Hindi to the disadvantage of local Kannada 
candidates, contrary to the policy of setting question papers in local regional language, English 
and Hindi.  
The earlier instances of injustice include: (i) Pri nting of railway tickets in Tamil and 
Telugu, leaving out Kannada. (ii) Denial of engines  and bogies to the farmers of North 
Karnataka for distribution of maize and chemical fertilizers.  
As a result, there was widespread agitation, lathi charge and arrests.  
For protesting peacefully against such injustices, the protestors were described as 'Dirty 
People'.  
This remark aggravated agitation leading to damaging of railway property.  
Since the Group 'D' posts carry meagre salary, the candidates from Bihar cannot feed 
themselves and their family back home. Hence, it is better to recruit the local candidates to 
such a low-paid Group 'D' posts. A national policy be evolved to reserve Group 'D' and 
clerical posts only for the local candidates, as was done in Karnataka's Accountant-General's 
Office earlier under similar circumstances, at the intervention of UOI.  
Pending framing of such a policy, I appeal to scrap the Group 'D' recruitment examination 
already held in Karnataka and recruitment people against the said posts.  
Need to frame a Scheme to benefit the poorer Sections of people falling in the APL  
SHRI MATILAL SARKAR (Tripura): It is observed that the allotment of numbers of 
BLP families to the States and Union Territories does not suffice for inclusion of all the poor 
families in BPL lists. A good number of poor people is left out of BPL lists and gets included 
in the APL lists. Thus it remains a fact that the set of poor people stands divided on Government 
policy. A remarkable section of poor people is outside the domain of benefits given to the 
BPL families, though they deserve these benefits.  
Besides the benefits of foodgrains at lower prices, the benefits of housing schemes and 
the like, some State Governments have also adopted more welfare schemes for the BPL 
categories. On all occasions, the poorer section belonging to APL lists continues to remain 
deprived of the benefits actually due to them.  
As the revision of the BPL lists is a complicated and time-taking process, I urge upon the 
Central Government to chalk out some sort of a mechanism in the APL category itself, so 
that the poorer sections in APL lists may enjoy wel fare schemes similar to the schemes 
enjoyed by BPL families, pending fresh survey of BPL and APL lists.  
Thank you, Sir.

- Concern over Justice meted out to alleged culprit s by Vigilants Communities  
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA (Rajasthan): Sir, I rise to draw the attention of this House 
to the increasing trend of meeting out vigilante ju stice as being reported from almost every 
part of the country. The alleged culprits were subjected to instant and severe violence, perhaps 
not commensurate with the crime. Often, such violence is abetted by rumours or motivated 
information, as was witnessed in the case of a teac her in Delhi. Such violence has often 
taken place in Bihar. There have been recurrent reports on the severe justice being meted out 
by commuity courts for the violation of community code. Such cases of vigilante justice, on 
the one hand, reflect popular desperation owing to delay in justice due to the complex and 
layered system of justice, and, on the other hand, also indicate the severe breakdown of civil 
policing and justice delivery system at the local level. While justice has to be the fundamental 
right of citizens in a civilized society, it is also enshrined as a set principle that such justice 
will be delivered after a due process as laid down in the law. At the same time, it is also 
essential that justice delivery be made more efficient and affordable. The current judicial set 
up must not become an excuse to prolong the deliver y of justice. The legitimate quest for 
justice must not be denied due to delay. Government must ensure that the supremacy of law 
always prevails and must involve communities and civil society against vigilante justice.

THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA): Before w e go to the next 
speaker, there is one Special Mention which is left out. Shri O.T. Lepcha.  
SPECIAL MENTIONS— Contd.  
Need to take effective measures to maintain communication link on the National 
Highway 31-A, during Calls of Bandh  
SHRI O.T. LEPCHA (Sikkim): Hon. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I would like to draw the kind 
attention of the Central Government to the disturba nce caused by some regional political 
parties of Darjeeling district in West Bengal resorting to frequent strikes, and as a result of 
that the entire communication system is paralysed and the people of Sikkim are the worst 
sufferers since 1985. 
Sir, as you are all aware, being a land-locked State, there is no air link, rail link and other 
alternative highways. The only life-line is National Highway 31-A. In this regard, it may be 
mentioned that whenever such type of a call for strike or bandh in this region is given by any 
political party in West Bengal, the entire transpor t and communication system is totally 
paralysed. This is a very serious matter and the Ce ntral Government should take effective 
and necessary steps to restore the communication system, especially on National Highway 
31 -A, in the interest of the people of Sikkim. The Government should intervene in the matter.  
Therefore, I urge upon the Central Government to look into the matter serious and take 
appropriate action in the interest of Sikkim State. Thank you.

SHRIC. RAMACHANDRAIAH (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, a very exhaustive and emotional discussion 
is being taking place in this august House. Sir, we can compromise with anything, but not with the 
integrity of the nation. It appears to be a very small thing, threatening the people to leave their 
State. But, it has got a tremendous impact also. It is like a cancer. It should not be allowed to spread 
to other parts of the country. Sir, every aberration in democracy is being done to divide our society 
and we havebeen accustomed to compromise with everything to continue in power. I have been 
seeing all the leaders of the political parties making a uniform appeal that such things should be 
condemned. Those persons, who are indulging in such violence should be punished, but why 
should not we practise outside? The same persons, who have participated in the debate, have made 
suggestions to the Government,  

 
 
 
 
238    Short Duration  [RAJYASABHA]  Discussion  
but why should not we try to restrain ourselves fro m making political captains by allowing people to 
indulge in such things? Such tentacles should not b e allowed to spread in the country, It is a very 
dangerous trend. It was there when I was a student in Chennai. I have seen the linguistic chauvinism 
that has prevailed which has caused the regional parochialism in Maharashtra. So, everything is being done 
to take political advantage. There is no exception. They should have dealt with it. I do not want to t ake 
advantage of the situation and I do not want to pol iticise the issue also. People who have indulged in  
violence are the perpetrators. But what is the role  of the Government? By keeping complacent, by 
keeping inactive, the Government has become abettor. The Government is equally responsible. If the 
persons, who have been indulging in such violations, which have posed a great threat to our democracy 
and integrity of the country, are the perpetrators,  the Government is abettor. We cannot restrain 
ourselves from accusing the Government and I do not  want to take their names and glorify them by 
taking their names in this august House. Why has th e Government restrained itself from taking 
immeditate action? Why has this strong message not been sent to the nation? Sir, these things should 
not be allowed to spread. The country is beset with so many problems-hunger, poverty, unemployment, 
economic inequality, extremism. Our energies, our intelligence and our resources should be conserved 
and consumed for solving these problems. Instead of doing that, we are trying to create more problems 
which pose a danger to the integrity of the country. Unless good and conducive atmosphere prevails in this 
country, it will be very difficult to get investmen ts. It will be difficult to get technology and crea te 
infrastructure. The Prime Minister has been saying that we should go for double-digit growth. But, if this 
state of affairs continues in the counrtry, I do not think any foreign investor will come and invest in this 
country. Bombay City has not been built by one person and not by Maharashtrians alone. It was built 
over centuries by so many people and different peop le are there. About 11 per cent people are Hindi-
speaking people in Maharashtra and 1.5 per cent Tel ugu-speaking people are there, and speaking a 
particular language is not a prohibitive affair. As per the Constitution, every citizen is entitled to move 
anywhere, to own the properties anywhere. We have got a freedom of trade. We can speak any language. 
We can follow any religious faith. Ours is a great democracy, very strong democracy with independent 
Judiciary, free Press, very dynamic electoral syste m and we have to conserve it and pass it on the 
posterity and the Government should strive to prote ct it. We should not allow this to be destroyed. I 
do not want to make any political speech, but it is  a sorry state of affairs. It should not be taken v ery 
lightly. People responsible for it are traitors of the country. They should be given the hardest 
punishment. If existing laws are not sufficient, th e entire House will join the Home Minister of this 
country in making a special legislation to punish them.

SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL: I object to this, Sir. (Interruptions) I object to this, Sir. 
(Interruptions) It is not necessary for him to raise this issue. (Interruptions) If he raise this issue, 
then, he shall have to hear my reply also. No Member is entitled to write to the Government 
servant. He can write to me. And, whatever letters he has written to me, I have replied to them.

DR. BARUN MUKHERJEE (West Bengal): Thank you, Sir. I rise to talk with agony and 
with great concern on this particular issue because this is one such issue which threatens our 
national integrity. It has happened now in Maharashtra. Previously, it happened in Assam. 
And, now, some people are even saying that one Maha rashtrian Government is there in a 
Hindi-speaking State. It is like an infectious dise ase and it will spread from one place to 
another. So, on behalf of our party, I strongly condemn this type of narrow regionalism.  

Short Duration  [5 MARCH 2008]  Discussion   263  
I would like to remind the hon. Members once more that during the Freedom Movement, 
long before, as early as in 1938, Negtaji Subhas Ch andra Bose in his historical Haripurra 
Speech told that there are menaces in our political and social history, that is, communalism, 
casteism and regionalism. We have seen that happening many times, in many places. So, this 
is one such instance where we are, again, facing all these things.  
As a son of Bengal, I know the agonies and pains of  division of a country. We have 
suffered it and we have experienced it. At the same time, as a son of Bengal I say that here is 
a place where people from all the States of the country are working. They are staying there 
for various reasons. In the giant jute mills, 10,00 0 to 14,000 people are working there. 
Mostly the Hindi speaking people are working there. Even people from South India are also 
there. We have great respect for Maharastra. During the Freedom Movement we used to say, 
Lal, Bal, and Pal. They were the three giants of th e Freedom Movement. Shri Lala Lajpat 
Rai was from Punjab, Shri Bal Gangadhar Tilak was from Maharashtra and Shri Bipin Chandra 
Pal was from Bengal. We used to pay our respect to thern. So, we hope that this parochialism 
is not there. It was the duty of the State Government, at least, I should say, to nip the problem 
in the bud. But, unfortunately, that has not been done. The Union Home Minister has taken 
steps at the right moment. We read in the newspapers that he warned the State Government 
to take action in this respect.  
So, before concluding, I would like to say that onl y various Government actions and 
police actions should be taken, but, creating some sort of awareness among the people is 
absolutely necessary. Some leading sociologists even say that more inter-caste marriages or 
inter-State marriages will develop affinity between  the people. So, that is the main 
thing... (Interruption)...  
MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Okay, okay.  
DR. BARUN MUKHERJEE: We all belong to one country. Let us keep continuing it. 
Thank you.  
MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Shri D. Raja. Please don't take more than three minutes. I 
am not going to allow more than that.  
SHRI D. RAJA (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I would like to formally state the position of my Party 
on that issue. What happended in Maharashtra or what is happening today should not have 
happended. Earlier, there were attacks against Tamil and South Indians, and now, we find 
attacks against the North Indians. What is happening there should not have happened. The 
greatness of our country lies in the tremendous div ersity it has got. Through this diversity 
only, our country is progressing. Having said this, I must say that we should address the root 
cause of the problem. Over these years, the policies pursued by the Governments at Delhi as 
well as in States have created a situation where you find the urban-rural divide and the rich-
poor divide growing at an alarming proportion. So, people migrate from palce to palce for 
livelihood to seek jobs and other things. There is our Constitution which provides that the 
citizens can move from one place to another and they can live there and they can seek jobs 
there. It is our Constitution. Nobody should act against this spirit of the Constitution. Nobody 
should curtail the freedom of our people migrating from place to place. But there are parochial 
forces, regional forces which are taking advantage. They are desperate. They have no other 
agenda, or, issue. They pick up such issues and target vulnerable sections. They are not only 
going for livelihood, but they also build assets th ere. Wherever they go, they build these 
cities. It happens in the case of Mumbai, it happens in the case of Chennai, it happens in the

case of Bangalore or any other city you take, for i nstance. These are all built by people 
together, collectively. That is where we should see  the strength of our nation. After all, 
Maharashtra is a pride of the nation. Maharashtra is a place where we had the great legends 
like Mahatma Phule, Dr. Ambedkar and Comrade Dange.  Mumbai was one of the pioneer 
places where the communist movement emerged. I must  say it. The entire working class 
movement began there; the trade union movement began there. That is why Maharashtra is 
a pride for us and Maharashtra should not witness s uch attacks against our own fellow 
citizens. Whoever does, they cannot take law into their hands. The Central Government and 
the State Government must take appropriate action whenever such parochial elements play

SHRI TAPAN KUMAR SEN (West Bengal) : Mr. Deputy Cha irman Sir, I join my 
colleagues in the House in condemning the incidents that have taken place in Maharashtra of 
attack against migrant people going to that State f or their bread and butter. I share their 
emotions. I am not going into the details; they have already been talked about. I just want to 
say, as I understand, that this is the handiwork of the forces who play divisive politics in the 
name of caste, religion, region and so on and so fo rth. They get the opportunity to play 
divisive politics in a situaiton of extreme vulnerability and restlessness in the society because 
of hunger, poverty and joblessness. Particularly, the search for job makes a man made and 
desperate enough and results in this kind of inter-State migration. Perhaps this is also a test 
of the degree of inclusiveness in our economic exercise that is taking place. In such a situaiton, 
such things and bound to happen and we will have to  guard and fight together against that 
kind of political opportunism. I would like to tell  the hon. Home Minister that what is 
particularly noticed here is a rabid failure of governance immediately after the incident took 
place and that inaction and non-responsiveness of the local government has exposed some 
kind of an indulgent attitude, may be out of some p olitical opportunism. That needs to be 
explained. No doubt, the Government of India has in tervened and tried to set things right, 
but the initial non-responsiveness is a serious things. We need to take that into account.  
The second, and the most important, point is that t his mobility and inter-State 
migration would further increase particularly in th e kind of economic situation that is 
prevailing. The Inter-State Migrant Workers Act is the most violated statue as on date in our 
country. In such a situation, unless special attention is given to see to it that the Inter-state 
Migrant Workers Act is properly implemented, I thin k the problem would multiply in the 
days to come. The Government needs to look into that aspect too.
